# Abstract

Northern Cascadia and Alaska (2,64M km², 68.756 active 5-arcminute cells) supported the densest pre-agricultural populations in northern North America along salmon-rich Pacific fjords, clam-garden archipelagos and upwelling Beringian shelves.

Reconstructed across five ecological divisions under CENTAUR-II from 10000BC to 1600AD, regional population rises from 1,35k in 10000BC to 25,7k in 5000BC, 119,7k at 0AD and a pre-contact plateau of 182k across 1500AD and 1550AD (6,9 persons per 100 km²), easing slightly to 181,5k by 1600AD.

Inhabitants remained heavily concentrated along the southern outer coast and Salish Sea: by 1500AD, the Salish Sea, Vancouver Island and Fraser-Columbia Plateau (39,6%) together with the Inside Passage, Haida Gwaii and Skeena-Nass Coast (25,3%) accounted for 64,8% of total population on 29,2% of land area, led in sub-regional density by the Salish-Fraser division (15,99 persons per 100 km²) and the Inside Passage (14,41 persons per 100 km²).

Spatial disaggregation pairs 225 catalogued settlement trajectories (461 ledger candidates with 234 duplicate-alias consolidations and 2 excluded non-habitation cave features) with a multi-registry North American radiocarbon composite (93.129 unique site-periods across 286.193 horizon site records, 3.833 domestic catchments spanning 15,52M km² with 2.570 active inhabited and 251 cross-frontier buffer catchments, 14,24x the 6.539-entry legacy baseline over 493.687 valid land cells covering 18,56M km²) calibrated via non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging (regularised $\tau_1 = 1,35$ across all 10 horizons from 13000BC to 1650AD, raw 1,519 to 1,6098 with horizon mean 1,5782, $\tau_2 = 2,9025$, effective short range 45,23 km to 47,94 km, raw nugget-to-sill 0, regularised 0,04 with $\eta = 0,0417$, WLS $R^2 = 0,9990$ to 0,9992), removing arbitrary provincial and international discontinuities across Alaska, Yukon, British Columbia and Washington.

# Background

## Ecological Asymmetry and Historiographic Context

Northern Cascadia and Alaska span one of the steepest ecological gradients in human prehistory. Whereas interior Yukon and northern Alaska resemble boreal Siberia in low terrestrial primary productivity and seasonal caribou mobility, the glaciated fjord belt from Kodiak Island to Puget Sound couples mild maritime rainfall with immense runs of anadromous Pacific salmon, halibut, herring, sea mammals and intertidal shellfish [@kroeber1939; @ames1999; @campbell2010archaeological].

Earlier continental syntheses often smoothed these contrasts across broad ethnohistoric zones, masking the sharp demographic break between sedentary coastal plank-house towns and sparse interior riverine bands. When coarse carrying-capacity averages are projected uniformly across cordilleran and coastal zones, dense littoral chiefdoms are flattened while subarctic muskeg basins appear artificially uniform.

CENTAUR-II partitions 2.638.604 km² into five physiographically coherent sub-regions bounded by major watersheds, mountain cordilleras and maritime upwelling shelves (Table \ref{tab:subregions}). Each division tracks a distinct ecological regime across 23 benchmark dates from late-glacial colonisation to protohistoric contact.

## Five Ecological Divisions

### Aleutian Archipelago, Kodiak and Gulf of Alaska Coast

The Aleutian Archipelago, Kodiak and Gulf of Alaska Coast (456.493 km², 17,3% of regional area) covers volcanic island chains and fjorded southern peninsulas occupied by Unangan (Aleut), Sugpiaq (Alutiiq) and Chugach maritime communities [@laughlin1980; @fitzhugh2003].

Ice-free coastal shelves, dense kelp forests and year-round sea-otter, seal and cod fisheries sustained dense village clusters along Kodiak Island and the eastern Aleutian arc (6,13 persons per 100 km² across the division by 1500AD), despite recurrent tectonic subsidence and tsunami hazards along the Aleutian trench [@shennan2018late; @vanderhoek2009role].

### Bering Sea Delta and North Slope Arctic Tundra

North and west of the Alaska Range, the Bering Sea Delta and North Slope Arctic Tundra (612.151 km², 23,2%) stretches from the Yukon-Kuskokwim wetlands across Seward Peninsula and Kotzebue Sound to the Chukchi and Beaufort whaling capes inhabited by Yup'ik and Inupiat societies [@larsen1948; @mason2016; @tremayne2017late].

Broad coastal deltaic wetlands and bowhead whale migration corridors along sea-ice leads concentrated marine villages along outer headlands, contrasting sharply with sparse seasonal caribou hunting across interior foothills [@tremayne2016large].

### Interior Yukon-Tanana Subarctic Basin

Between the St. Elias-Coast Mountains and the Mackenzie divide lies the Interior Yukon-Tanana Subarctic Basin (800.435 km², 30,3%), a vast continental sprawl of boreal spruce taiga, permafrost uplands and glacial river valleys held by Northern Athabaskan groups [@holmes2001; @morlan2003].

Long winter freezes and dispersed moose, caribou and freshwater fishery resources kept regional densities low, though alpine ice-patch finds confirm enduring seasonal procurement and trade across coastal mountain passes [@murchie2015investigating].

### Inside Passage, Haida Gwaii and Skeena-Nass Coast

Southward along the Pacific coast, the Inside Passage, Haida Gwaii and Skeena-Nass Coast (319.248 km², 12,1%) comprises the outer archipelagos and coastal valleys of Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian and Nuxalk peoples, where deep cedar forests and Prince Rupert Harbour shell middens anchored hereditary house groups [@matson1995; @cui2013ancient; @letham2015holocene].

Sheltered fjords, prolific spring eulachon runs at river mouths and outer-island kelp beds fostered dense multi-lineage towns tied together by canoe navigation and crest-based redistribution [@ames1999].

### Salish Sea, Vancouver Island and Fraser-Columbia Plateau

Finally, the Salish Sea, Vancouver Island and Fraser-Columbia Interior Plateau (450.277 km², 17,1%) joins the rich sheltered inland sea of Vancouver Island and the Strait of Georgia with winter pit-house canyon settlements along the Fraser and Thompson rivers [@hayden1997; @boyd1999; @holmes2022ancestral].

Warm rain-shadow lowlands, intertidal shellfish terraces and massive sockeye salmon migrations through narrow Fraser canyons sustained the largest regional population cluster north of the Columbia estuary [@campbell2010archaeological].

## Coastal Mariculture and Marine Resource Management

Coastal intensification sharply differentiates the archaeological record of Northern Cascadia from adjacent boreal regions. Across Haida Gwaii, the Dundas Islands and Quadra Island, intertidal rock-walled clam gardens expanded bivalve productivity by stabilising beach terraces over at least 3.500 to 3.800 years [@smith2019years; @holmes2022ancestral; @letham2015holocene].

Coupled with multi-millennial herring fisheries, tidal stone fish traps and salmon stream stewardship [@campbell2010archaeological; @pinkerton2019reconciling], these engineered marine landscapes supported corporate village lineages capable of absorbing local seismic shocks, river avulsions and mid-Holocene cooling episodes without prolonged demographic collapse.

In contrast, interior and Arctic communities relied on mobile seasonal scheduling tied to caribou migration routes, permafrost thaw-lake fisheries and coastal sea-ice leads [@holmes2001; @tremayne2016large]. Understanding how those two subsistence regimes shifted in relative demographic weight across ten millennia is the central question addressed by this regional reconstruction.

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Partitioning and Demographic Anchors

Each of the five sub-regional time series spans 23 benchmarks between 10000BC and 1600AD. The cadence comprises millennial intervals from 10000BC to 0AD, bicentennial steps from 0AD to 1000AD, centennial steps through 1500AD and half-century resolution at 1550AD and 1600AD.

Sub-regional benchmark totals combine ethnohistoric carrying-capacity baselines at contact [@kroeber1939; @ubelaker2006] with archaeological house-pit counts, shell-midden volumes and regional radiocarbon summed probability distributions [@kelly2025; @ames1999; @fitzhugh2003].

Every sub-regional estimate carries an explicit symmetric +/- 8% uncertainty interval from 10000BC to 1600AD, reflecting spread across alternative house-occupancy assumptions and contact-nadir multipliers [@ubelaker2006; @boyd1999].

## Multi-Registry Radiocarbon Composite and Matérn Kriging

Within each sub-regional mask, rural habitation weights derive from a continental North American radiocarbon composite spanning 493.687 valid terrestrial 5-arcminute cells covering 18.561.382 km² (18,56M km²), of which 78.938 to 149.138 active inhabited non-wasteland cells carry non-zero rural density across 10 horizons (13000BC to 1650AD). Rather than relying on a single archaeological repository, the underlying point surface integrates global radiocarbon catalogues (c14bazAAR and p3k14c) [@bird2022p3k14c] with the Canadian Archaeological Radiocarbon Database (CARD), United States state site files, Alaska Heritage Resources Survey records, British Columbia site registers, Greenland *Nunniffiit* inventories and cultural resource management syntheses.

After spatial and chronological deduplication by catchment and 200-year bin, the North American composite contains 93.129 unique site-period records (286.193 horizon site records across all intervals) distributed across 3.833 domestic catchments (15.517.268 km² or 15,52M km²; 2.570 active inhabited catchments, 67,05% catchment coverage). This multi-registry integration raises effective observation density to 14,24x the 6.539-entry legacy c14bazAAR baseline alone.

Across mainland North America and Greenland, domestic catchments exhibit an equivalent circular radius ($r = \sqrt{A/\pi}$) median of 29,48 km and a 90th-percentile radius of 40,95 km overall (29,3 km median and 39,85 km 90th-percentile across active inhabited catchments). To prevent artificial edge drop-offs along the Bering Strait, the Alaska-Yukon frontier and the forty-ninth parallel, 251 cross-frontier buffer catchments condition Chukotka, Kamchatka and northern Washington up to 300 km beyond the module perimeter.

Biophysical weighted least-squares covariates capture coastal proximity, 13,5 km fluvial distance decay, terrain slope and ecological zone productivity before 2D Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging across 10 Holocene horizons (13000BC to 1650AD), anchored to regional summed probability curves [@kelly2025].

## Settlement Subtraction and Boundary Feathering

To prevent double counting between nucleated villages and dispersed rural populations, 225 catalogued settlement trajectories are extracted from primary monographs and heritage inventories and pinned to exact WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year, active settlement populations inside each sub-region are summed and subtracted from the sub-regional total.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to the kriged surface inside the areal mask. Two passes of a 4-pixel separable smoothing filter across sub-regional and inter-module borders eliminate artificial step cliffs across the Coast Mountains, the Alaska-Yukon meridian and the British Columbia-Washington divide.

# Testing and Validation

Three quantitative checks govern the Northern Cascadia and Alaska module prior to compilation:

1. **Variogram Sharpness and Fit**: Across all 10 horizons (13000BC to 1650AD; 78.938 to 149.138 active cells) of the North American Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) surface, the regularised dimensionless short-range scale parameter holds at $\tau_1 = 1,35$ on every horizon (raw per-horizon range 1,519 to 1,6098, horizon mean 1,5782, below the 1,8 ceiling) and the secondary scale holds at $\tau_2 = 2,9025$ (2,9), yielding an effective short range of 45,23 km to 47,94 km (mean 47 km). Raw nugget-to-sill equals 0 across all ten horizons, and regularised nugget-to-sill holds uniformly at 0,04 ($\eta = 0,0417$, well below the 0,45 ceiling). Weighted least-squares covariates remain active across all ten horizons, yielding residual $R^2$ values from 0,999 to 0,9992, summarised by horizon in Table \ref{tab:kriging}.
2. **Gazetteer and Ledger Reconciliation**: Cross-checking the 225 included settlement records against the 461 candidates in the source ledger confirms 0 unaccounted records, 0 coordinate bounding-box violations and 236 documented exclusions (234 duplicate-alias consolidations merged within 2 km into canonical records such as Ipiutak, Cape Krusenstern, Marpole and Yuquot, alongside 2 non-habitation cave exclusions at Eagle Cave and On Your Knees Cave). Sub-regional coverage spans all five divisions: 44 sites in Aleutians-Kodiak, 39 in Arctic Alaska, 21 in Interior Yukon-Tanana, 63 along the Inside Passage and Outer Coast and 58 across the Salish Sea and Fraser-Columbia Plateau.
3. **Cross-Frontier Seam Continuity**: Cross-border transitions linking Northern Cascadia and Alaska with Northern Canada and Greenland to the northeast, the Canadian Prairies to the east and the Pacific Northwest hydrological unit to the south exhibit smooth coastal and riverine density gradients without rectilinear boundary artifacts.

# Results

## Early Holocene Colonisation and Beringian Refugia (10000BC to 5000BC)

### Beringian Interior Corridors and Refugia

During the terminal Pleistocene and Early Holocene, the ice-free interior valleys of eastern Beringia and the emerging Pacific littoral formed two contrasting colonisation fronts. In 10000BC, regional population stood at 1,35k (1,24k to 1,46k), still tethered to the unglaciated steppe-tundra of the Yukon and Tanana drainage rather than the glaciated fjords to the south.

Interior Yukon-Tanana (450) and Bering-North Slope (400) hunter-gatherers together accounted for nearly two-thirds of the initial regional total. Their seasonal camps clustered along bluff overlooks and river confluences at Swan Point (150 peak), Broken Mammoth (55 peak), Little John (45 peak) and Bluefish Caves (20 peak), followed soon after by Healy Lake (95 peak from 9500BC) and Dry Creek (45 peak from 9800BC) [@holmes2001; @morlan2003; @cook1996].

Along the outer coast, early marine foragers followed the retreating Cordilleran ice margin across emerging islands and drowned shelves. Even in 10000BC, small littoral bands already numbered 250 inhabitants on the Aleutian-Kodiak shelf, 150 along the Inside Passage and 100 in the Salish-Fraser corridor [@ames1999; @mobley1988holocene].

### Post-Glacial Warming and Pacific Littoral Shift

As post-glacial warming opened interior valleys and stabilised outer-coast fjords, total population doubled from 1,35k in 10000BC to 2,6k in 9000BC and more than tripled again to 8,9k by 7000BC. Over these three millennia, demographic momentum shifted decisively away from Beringian grasslands toward the Pacific rim.

On the Aleutian-Kodiak shelf, blade-and-microblade marine foragers settled Anangula (60 peak from 6500BC) and Chaluka (520 peak from 6500BC), alongside Ugashik Narrows (160 peak from 7000BC) and Ocean Bay (95 peak from 4500BC) [@laughlin1980; @vanderhoek2009role]. Year-round sea-mammal hunting, sea-bird rookeries and ice-free headlands gave these maritime settlements an ecological buffer rarely matched in interior caribou country.

Along the central and northern British Columbia coast and Southeast Alaska, early coastal occupation began at Kilgii Gwaay (40 peak from 8500BC), Namu (8500BC onward, rising to 540 peak), Ground Hog Bay 2 (75 peak from 8000BC), Richardson Island (45 peak from 7500BC) and Hidden Falls (7500BC onward, 160 peak) [@matson1995; @campbell2010archaeological]. Farther south, early Fraser Canyon salmon fishing at Milliken (7500BC onward, 340 peak) and Glenrose Cannery (6500BC onward, 290 peak) anchored southern riverine corridors as Cordilleran lakes drained.

By 5000BC, regional population reached 25,7k, a nineteen-fold increase above the 10000BC baseline. At that midpoint, Salish-Fraser (9,5k, 37%) and the Inside Passage (7k, 27,2%) already held nearly two-thirds of all inhabitants, leaving the Aleutians (4,2k), Interior Yukon-Tanana (2,9k) and Arctic Alaska (2,1k) as slower-growing northern flanks.

## Middle Holocene Maritime Consolidation (4000BC to 1000BC)

### Outer-Coast Shell Middens and Salmon Storage

Between 4000BC (37,8k) and 1000BC (96,5k), stabilised sea levels along Southeast Alaska and northern British Columbia coincided with sustained expansion of Pacific salmon runs and coastal storage economies [@mobley1988holocene; @campbell2010archaeological]. Once estuarine mudflats matured after 4000BC, annual spawning returns could be smoked, dried and banked across entire extended households.

On the outer coast and Dundas Islands archipelago, shell-midden hamlets proliferated into permanent winter villages such as Boardwalk (2500BC onward, rising to 560 peak), Hidden Falls (160), Laxgalts'ap (1000BC onward) and Lachane (1000BC onward) [@matson1995; @letham2015holocene]. Ancient mitochondrial DNA recovered from mid-Holocene individuals at Prince Rupert Harbour and Lucy Island confirms long-term local matrilineal continuity across these coastal settlements over several millennia [@cui2013ancient].

### Clam-Garden Mariculture, Pit-Houses and Arctic Foragers

Farther south, mariculture engineering transformed foreshore productivity across sheltered channels. Rock-walled clam gardens along the Salish Sea, Broughton Archipelago and Quadra Island expanded intertidal butter-clam and littleneck habitat from at least 1800BC onward, anchoring multi-family winter villages at Yuquot (2300BC onward), Tsawwassen (2000BC onward), Marpole (1000BC onward) and Scowlitz [@smith2019years; @holmes2022ancestral].

Simultaneously, semi-subterranean winter pit-house aggregates took shape in the Fraser Canyon at Keatley Creek (1000BC onward), where wind-funnelled canyon benches made mass salmon drying feasible on an industrial scale [@hayden1997]. Farther north, Kachemak and Ocean Bay maritime villages lifted Aleutian-Kodiak numbers from 6,2k in 4000BC to 16,5k in 1000BC [@fitzhugh2003].

Across the far northern tundra, Arctic Small Tool and Denbigh groups pushed Bering and North Slope coastal numbers from 2,8k in 4000BC to 8,5k in 1000BC. Even in Arctic waters, however, settlement expansion tracked periodic swings in terrestrial caribou biomass alongside marine seal and walrus productivity [@tremayne2016large; @tremayne2017late].

## Late Holocene Chiefdoms, Plateau Villages and Arctic Whaling (0AD to 1500AD)

### Regional Consolidation and Alpine Exchange

By 0AD, Northern Cascadia and Alaska reached 119,7k inhabitants, almost half of all pre-contact growth after 10000BC having already occurred before the Christian era. Salish-Fraser held 48k (40,1%) and the Tlingit-Haida-Tsimshian Outer Coast held 32k (26,7%), joined by 19,5k in Aleutians-Kodiak, 12k across Bering-North Slope and 8,2k in Interior Yukon-Tanana.

Over the next fifteen centuries, total population rose more gradually by 52% to 166,9k in 1000AD and 182k in 1500AD. Rather than pioneering empty landscapes, late Holocene societies deepened social stratification, fortified defensive ridge settlements and intensified inter-regional exchange across coastal passes [@ames1999; @matson1995; @murchie2015investigating]. Cryogenic alpine wooden artefacts and ancient DNA recovered from southern Yukon ice patches attest to durable trade and biological ties linking interior Athabaskan hunters with northern Northwest Coast chiefdoms [@murchie2015investigating].

### Salish Sea, Fraser Canyon and Outer-Coast Towns

In the Salish Sea and Fraser Canyon, plank-house towns and dense pit-house villages reached peak dimensions during the first and early second millennia AD. Marpole peaked at 1,45k residents (1500AD), Keatley Creek reached 1,4k (1000AD), Yuquot climbed from 420 at 0AD to 1,15k by 1500AD (1,2k in 1600AD), Bridge River Pithouse Metropolis reached 1,1k (1050AD; nearby Bridge River 820), Keatley Creek Pithouse Town reached 950 (1100AD), Victoria (Cadboro Bay) reached 620 (1600AD) and Ts'ishaa Capital reached 610 (1500AD) [@hayden1997; @ames1999].

Along the Skeena, Nass and outer archipelagos, Tsimshian, Haida and Tlingit towns anchored corporate lineage territories sustained by monumental red-cedar architecture, salmon storage and intertidal sea gardens. Major winter agglomerations stood at Laxgalts'ap (920 peak), Gitwangak (720), Sitka (680), Lax Kw'alaams (610), Massett (580), Bella Coola (540), Wrangell (520), Skidegate (510) and SGang Gwaay (480) [@matson1995; @holmes2022ancestral; @pinkerton2019reconciling].

### Kodiak Villages, Arctic Whalers and Interior Athabaskans

On Kodiak Island and the Alaska Peninsula, Late Kachemak and Koniag intensification lifted Karluk from 300 at 0AD to 550 in 1000AD and 820 by 1600AD. Across neighbouring bays and salmon streams, nucleated villages grew at Izembek (540 peak), Chaluka (520 peak), Uyak (390), Nushagak (380), Naknek (380) and Port Moller (360) [@fitzhugh2003; @vanderhoek2009role].

Meanwhile, along the Bering Sea and North Slope tundra, Norton, Old Bering Sea, Ipiutak, Birnirk and Thule whaling innovations doubled Arctic Alaska population from 12k at 0AD to 21,8k in 1000AD and 24k by 1500AD. Large coastal whalebone mounds concentrated populations at Ipiutak (800 peak at 600AD, 550 in 1500AD), Utqiagvik (560 in 1500AD, 620 peak), Gambell (580 peak), Wales (520), Kukulik (520), Cape Krusenstern (480) and Kotzebue (440) [@larsen1948; @mason2016; @tremayne2017late].

Across the interior Yukon-Tanana taiga, Athabaskan salmon-weir and caribou-fence bands expanded modestly from 8,2k at 0AD to 12k in 1500AD. Semi-permanent gathering settlements anchored regional circuits at Rat Indian Creek Town (310 peak), Fort Yukon (250), Klondike-Tr'ochëk (220), Nenana (210), Circle (200), Carcross (170) and Klo-kut (170) [@holmes2001; @tremayne2016large].

## Protohistoric Plateau and Early Contact Threshold (1500AD to 1600AD)

Aggregate population across Northern Cascadia and Alaska plateaued at 182k across 1500AD and 1550AD (6,9 persons per 100 km²) before declining marginally by 0,27% (500 inhabitants) to 181,5k in 1600AD. That terminal pause marks the transition from purely endogenous demographic dynamics to indirect continental disturbance.

The slight sixteenth-century dip concentrates entirely in the Salish Sea and Fraser-Columbia Plateau (72k to 71,5k), reflecting early indirect diffusion of Old World pathogens along Columbia-Plateau and Pacific trade corridors ahead of direct European arrival [@campbell1990; @boyd1999; @ubelaker2006]. Farther north, relative geographic insulation preserved pre-contact stability across the Aleutians (28k), Arctic Alaska (24k), the Tlingit-Haida Outer Coast (46k) and Interior Yukon (12k) through 1600AD, leaving 181,5k regional inhabitants on the eve of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century maritime contact. Table \ref{tab:master} compiles the twenty-three-benchmark regional series with +/- 8% uncertainty intervals.

# Limitations

## Survey Bias and Interior Taiga Sampling

Four structural constraints qualify the Northern Cascadia and Alaska reconstruction. First, archaeological radiocarbon density concentrates heavily along accessible highway corridors, hydroelectric reservoirs, oil-pipeline transects and coastal cultural resource surveys in southern British Columbia and south-central Alaska [@bird2022p3k14c; @holmes2001].

Interior Yukon-Tanana muskeg, high alpine glaciers and remote western Aleutian islands remain comparatively under-sampled [@vanderhoek2009role]. Although non-stationary Matérn kriging borrows covariance strength across 3.833 domestic catchments (2.570 active) and 251 cross-frontier buffers, low-density taiga basins still retain wider relative interpolation variance than coastal shell-midden zones.

## Eustatic Submergence, Reservoir Offsets and Interval Width

Second, relative sea-level fluctuations, glacio-isostatic rebound in Southeast Alaska and megathrust coseismic subsidence around Kodiak and the Gulf of Alaska have drowned or eroded large stretches of pre-5000BC shoreline [@mobley1988holocene; @shennan2018late; @letham2015holocene]. Early coastal populations between 10000BC and 6000BC therefore appear lower in terrestrial point inventories than later shell-midden towns perched above modern high-tide marks.

Third, variable marine radiocarbon reservoir offsets (Delta-R) across upwelling Aleutian, Bering and Dixon Entrance waters complicate phase boundary precision when marine shell and sea-mammal collagen dates are aggregated into 200-year bins [@tremayne2017late; @fitzhugh2003].

Fourth, the uniform +/- 8% intervals around sub-regional benchmarks summarise aggregate ethnohistoric and carrying-capacity uncertainty rather than site-by-site Bayesian floor-area error distributions [@ubelaker2006; @boyd1999]. Improved terrestrial-marine paired dating and intertidal survey will narrow early Holocene coastal confidence bounds in future revisions.

# Conclusion

## Long-Run Maritime Transformation

Northern Cascadia and Alaska trace a ten-millennium transition from sparse late-glacial Beringian hunting bands (1,35k in 10000BC) to one of pre-agricultural North America's most populous maritime zones (182k in 1500AD to 1550AD, 181,5k in 1600AD). Post-glacial warming flipped the continental demographic centre of gravity from steppe-tundra river bluffs toward ice-free Pacific fjords within three millennia.

Coastal intensification around salmon fisheries, clam gardens and sea-mammal hunting created a durable spatial asymmetry. By 1500AD, the three Pacific coastal and cordilleran divisions (Salish-Fraser, Inside Passage and Aleutians-Kodiak) held 80,2% of regional inhabitants on 46,5% of land area, led by 15,99 persons per 100 km² across the Salish Sea and Fraser-Columbia Plateau and 14,41 per 100 km² along the Inside Passage (6,13 in Aleutians-Kodiak and 3,92 in Arctic Alaska), compared with 1,5 persons per 100 km² across the Yukon-Tanana boreal interior.

## Composite Synthesis and Protohistoric Threshold

Reconciling 225 catalogued settlements against multi-registry Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging surfaces calibrated across 93.129 North American site-periods eliminates provincial and international seam artifacts. Adjacent transitions into northern Canada, the Canadian prairies and the Columbia plateau remain continuous without arbitrary border steps.

On the eve of European contact in 1600AD, northern maritime and subarctic regions remained untouched at peak populations (28k Aleutians, 24k Arctic Alaska, 46k Outer Coast, 12k Interior Yukon), while only the Salish-Fraser corridor registered an incipient protohistoric dip (72k to 71,5k).
